title: Telling about yesterday, planning tomorrow

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kumusta ang weekend mo?
dialogs.intro: Monday morning in class. Before the lesson starts, everyone swaps weekend stories.

notes: **Telling a story in Tagalog uses almost entirely the "done" form.** *Pumunta*, *kumain*, *naglakad*, *bumili*, *natulog* — all completed aspect. The exact time is given once at the start (*noong Sabado*) and not repeated. This is a big saving compared with languages that must mark time on every verb.
**Tapos is the most-used story connector.** It means "then", and in conversation it shows up in nearly every second sentence. The more formal version: *pagkatapos* (after that).

**Habang means "while"** and is always followed by the "ongoing" form: *habang naglalakad*, *habang kumakain*, *habang natutulog*. Note that the aspect changes — this is where the "ongoing" form shows up most often in past-tense stories.
**Bago means "before"** and takes the basic form: *bago sumikat ang araw*, *bago kumain*, *bago matulog*. The same word also means "new" — told apart by its position in the sentence, not by sound.
**Kaya here means "so, therefore"** and links cause with effect: *Pagod ako, kaya natulog ako agad.* It's the same word that means "able" in unit 16, told apart by stress and position.
**Balak and plano both mean plan.** *Balak* is more Tagalog and more casual; *plano*, from Spanish, is slightly more formal. The structure is the same as *gusto*: *balak **kong** pumunta*.
**Sana!** standing alone as an answer means "I hope so" — a warm yet noncommittal reply. Very useful when you can't yet be sure.
**May pasok ako** means "I have school/work to attend". *Walang pasok* means a day off, and *Walang pasok bukas!* is one of the happiest sentences in the Philippines, usually because of a typhoon.

**Nakita namin** comes from the root *kita* (seen) with the prefix *na-*: a form marking something that **happens by chance or is successfully done**. It appears constantly in stories: *nakita* (saw, caught sight of), *narinig* (heard), *nakain* (managed to eat).

grammars.title: Story connectors
body: Twenty units have given you verbs, markers and particles. What's left is the glue that joins sentences into a story.

head: Word
Meaning
Followed by
Example
rows: a sentence or a basic verb
Pagod ako, kaya umuwi na ako.

after: The most common story order: **time phrase → verb → doer → the rest**. *Noong Sabado, pumunta kami sa Tagaytay.*
If you run out of connectors, *tapos* can almost always be used. Native speakers lean on it too.
To start a story: *Alam mo ba…?* ("you know what…?") or *May kuwento ako.* ("I have a story.")

grammars.title: Stating plans
body: Plans are expressed with the "coming" form or with one of the following openers.

head: Pattern
Example
Translation
Tone
rows: gentle, often followed by a reason

after: *Baka* is the safest way to state a plan that isn't settled — and in the Philippines, where a direct refusal is considered rude, it often also means "probably not".
The sentence *Sige, text kita.* ("Okay, I'll text you") works the same way: friendly, open, noncommittal.
To ask about someone's plans: *Ano ang balak mo?* or *Ano ang gagawin mo bukas?*

blocks.text: Read the following paragraphs out loud. Every word in them has appeared in this book, and if you can follow them without looking at the translation, you've reached the end of A1.

blocks.title: Ang araw ko kahapon
items: *Gumising ako ng alas-sais ng umaga. Naligo ako, tapos nag-almusal ng kanin at itlog. Umalis ako ng bahay ng alas-siyete at sumakay ng jeep papuntang paaralan.*
*Nag-aral kami ng Tagalog hanggang alas-onse. Mahirap ang leksyon, pero masaya. Pagkatapos ng klase, kumain kami ni Ana sa karinderya. Sinigang ang ulam namin, at unlimited ang kanin.*
*Sa hapon, pumunta ako sa palengke. Bumili ako ng prutas at gulay. Nakalimutan ko ang pera ko kaya bumalik pa ako sa bahay — nakakainis!*
*Umuwi ako ng alas-singko. Naglinis ako ng kwarto, tapos nagpahinga. Natulog ako ng alas-diyes, pagod pero kontento.*

blocks.text: Translation: *I woke up at six in the morning. I showered, then had rice and eggs for breakfast. I left the house at seven and took a jeepney to school. We studied Tagalog until eleven. The lesson was hard, but fun. After class, Ana and I ate at a karinderya. Our dish was sinigang, and the rice was unlimited. In the afternoon, I went to the market. I bought fruit and vegetables. I forgot my money, so I had to go back home — how annoying! I got home at five. I cleaned my room, then rested. I went to bed at ten, tired but content.*

The prefix **nakaka-** forms adjectives meaning "making you …": *nakakainis* (annoying), *nakakapagod* (tiring), *nakakagutom* (making you hungry), *nakakatuwa* (delightful). This pattern is very productive and very popular with young Filipinos.

blocks.title: Congratulations, you've reached the end
items: Twenty units ago you didn't know that *ang* existed. Now you can greet, shop, order food, ride a jeepney, tell about yesterday and state your plans for tomorrow.
What you don't have yet is speed — and that comes from no book. It comes from hearing people talk and from daring to make mistakes in front of people who don't mind.
*Maraming salamat sa pag-aaral. Kaya mo 'yan — magaling ka na!*
